title: Rebuilding A Collapsed Bivalve Population, Restoring Seagrass Meadows, and Eradicating Harmful Algal Blooms In A Temperate Lagoon Using Spawner Sanctuaries
organism: hard clam → brown tide (Aureococcus), total chl
scale: Shinnecock Bay NY, 64 plots of ~1,850 m²
result: Bay filtration time fell from ≤3 months to 10 days; brown tide <10⁴ cells/mL in 2018-21 vs 0.3-1.9×10⁶ in 2007-16 (correlational).
env_effects: Clam densities rose 18× and harvests 16×; chl a fell significantly in the western bay.

title: Effect of the northern quahog Mercenaria mercenaria on the development of blooms of the brown tide alga Aureococcus anophagefferens
result: No-clam tanks passed 600,000 cells/mL; tanks with many clams were 100× lower; clearing ~40% of tank volume per day was enough.
env_effects: No rise in total biomass and no species shift.

title: Facilitation of seagrass Zostera marina productivity by suspension-feeding bivalves
organism: hard clam, oyster, mussel → natural phytoplankton
result: Chl a significantly lower with bivalves (p<0.05).
env_effects: Light penetration higher; eelgrass leaf growth +48 ± 9.3% at the highest bivalve density.

title: Application of filtration rate models to field populations of bivalves: an assessment using experimental mesocosms
result: Gross sedimentation +58% with clams; models using natural-seston rates fit, while maximum lab rates overestimated sedimentation by up to 10×.
env_effects: Extra sedimentation: 32% clam assimilation, 47% benthic respiration, 21% permanent biodeposits.

title: Efficiency of particle retention and filtration rate in 6 species of Northeast American bivalves
organism: 6 NE American bivalves incl. hard clam and oyster
result: Clam retains 100% of particles >4 µm, oyster 100% >5-6 µm and 50% at 2 µm; coefficient a in F=aW^b is 1.24 (clam) vs ~6.x (oyster; abstract digits partly unreadable).
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Comparison of feeding and biodeposition of three bivalves at different food levels
organism: mussel, oyster, hard clam → food suspensions
result: Feeding ranked clam < oyster < mussel at every food level; clam % removal fell at high food.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Bivalve Filter Feeding: Variability and Limits of the Aquaculture Biofilter
venue: Shellfish Aquaculture and the Environment, pp. 81-124
result: Oyster median clearance 3.00 L g⁻¹ h⁻¹ (as reported), 1.09 L ind⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 60 mm; most studies deplete <30% of particles.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: On measurement of filtration rate in bivalves-the stony road to reliable data: review and interpretation | The estimation of filtering rate from the clearance of suspensions (doi:10.1007/BF00355716)
venue: Mar Ecol Prog Ser (Riisgård 2001); Mar Biol 2:356 (Coughlan 1969)
result: Conflicting clearance data come partly from misused methods; Coughlan 1969 gives the control-corrected exponential clearance formula (via Cranford 2011, de Silva 2023).
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Effects of the harmful alga Margalefidinium (aka Cochlodinium) polykrikoides on clearance rates of the hard clam, Mercenaria mercenaria
organism: hard clam (10-20 mm) → Margalefidinium, Rhodomonas, Gymnodinium aureolum
result: Clams cleared the HAB at ≤1,000 cells/mL but clearance ≈0 at ≥1,500 cells/mL; non-harmful G. aureolum was cleared as fast as Rhodomonas.
env_effects: No change in opening or closing behaviour.

title: DIVERSE FEEDING RESPONSES OF FIVE SPECIES OF BIVALVE MOLLUSC WHEN EXPOSED TO THREE SPECIES OF HARMFUL ALGAE
organism: Mytilus edulis, Crassostrea virginica, Mya arenaria, Mercenaria mercenaria, Argopecten irradians -> Alexandrium fundyense, Prorocentrum minimum, Heterosigma akashiwo vs Rhodomonas sp.
scale: lab containers, NOAA Milford CT, May-Oct 2005
duration: 1 h clearance-rate incubations; 4 h behaviour and biodeposit observations
result: Clearance of HAB cells was either equal to or higher than clearance of Rhodomonas in every mixed-diet combination (no rejection of HAB cells); e.g. quahogs and scallops cleared A. fundyense faster than Rhodomonas, oysters cleared P. minimum faster. H. akashiwo clearance could not be measured because the cells swarmed and aggregated.
env_effects: Intact, undigested (possibly viable) HAB cells and temporary cysts of A. fundyense appeared in feces/pseudofeces of most species; oysters stayed mostly closed during 4 h exposures and produced no biodeposits with H. akashiwo; quahogs partly closed with A. fundyense.
key_details: Lab feeding study with five bivalve species exposed for 1 h to A. fundyense or P. minimum alone, Rhodomonas alone, or a mix, with empty-shell and no-shell controls (no algal loss in controls); ANOVA with LSD post hoc. Clearance rates were species- and alga-specific; the presence of Rhodomonas did not change clearance of HAB cells. H. akashiwo concentrations rose in no-shell controls due to swarming, so its clearance was not quantified. Biodeposits from most bivalves contained many intact HAB cells and A. fundyense temporary cysts, implying possible repackaging rather than destruction of HAB cells.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's 'HAB cells mostly retained preferentially' is overstated: clearance of HAB vs Rhodomonas was either not different or higher for HAB. H. akashiwo clearance was not measurable. Oysters were mostly closed with all three HABs (not only Heterosigma).

title: Clearance rates and toxin accumulation by North Atlantic bivalves during harmful algal blooms caused by the dinoflagellate, Dinophysis acuminata, in NY, USA, estuaries
organism: oyster, hard clam, mussel → Dinophysis acuminata
scale: 60-min clearance tests in 1 L stirred beakers of whole bloom water (10 bivalves per species, 3 bivalve-free control beakers) at Cold Spring Harbor and Jockey Creek, plus field-deployed bivalves at 3 NY sites (2021-2022)
duration: 60 min clearance trials; toxins tracked for ~6 weeks in deployed bivalves
result: Clearance on D. acuminata: oyster 1.69, mussel 0.46, clam 0.41 L h⁻¹ g⁻¹.
env_effects: M. edulis DST loads (265 ng OA + DTX1 per g) exceeded the FDA closure guideline (160 ng/g) for three weeks in 2022; oysters accumulated the most PTX2; toxins persisted ~6 weeks.
key_details: Bivalves starved 24 h were placed individually in 1 L beakers of raw Dinophysis bloom water (10 per species, 3 control beakers without bivalves) and cleared for 60 min, with Chl-a and Dinophysis counts at 0 and 60 min. All species cleared D. acuminata faster than Chl-a; oysters (1.69 +/- 1.34 L/h/g) were significantly faster than mussels (0.46 +/- 0.32) and hard clams (0.41 +/- 0.24). Separately deployed bivalves plus wild ribbed mussels accumulated DSTs and pectenotoxins, with blue mussels over the FDA guideline for three weeks. The study measures grazing and toxin risk, not bloom reduction.

title: Temporal Variability in Phytoplankton Removal by a Commercial, Suspended Eastern Oyster Nursery and Effects on Local Plankton Dynamics
scale: commercial FLUPSY (4 units x 10 upweller silos), East Creek off Great Peconic Bay, NY
result: Median weight-specific clearance 0.95 L/h/g during active growth (12 Jun-21 Jul); chlorophyll a removal across the FLUPSY had a season median of 6.45% (15.38% in the growth period, 24-h max 40%). Whole-FLUPSY clearance (median 3.64x10^5 L/h) would need ~18 days to clear the 1.6x10^5 m3 embayment, so no large impact on local phytoplankton.
env_effects: Cochlodinium polykrikoides (~100 cells/mL from 22 Jul) coincided with unstable, low feeding, no growth and higher oyster mortality; a Peridinium quinquecorne bloom (1,460 cells/mL) coincided with pseudofeces release in early June. Negative removal values (biodeposit release) occurred; diel clearance lows (0.32 and 0.45 L/h/g) coincided with lowest and highest DO/pH.
key_details: Field monitoring of inflow/outflow of a commercial oyster-seed FLUPSY at 15-min resolution through summer 2010. Environmental variables explained 58% of day-to-day feeding variability (multiple regression); clearance rose with O2 saturation up to 150%. Diel clearance peaked at 2.21 L/h/g (21:30) and bottomed at 0.32 L/h/g (07:40). Percent chlorophyll removal was highly variable, with a season median of 6.45% and negative values when biodeposits were released. Authors conclude the FLUPSY could not meaningfully reduce embayment phytoplankton because of replenishment by growth and exchange.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacked the percent chlorophyll removal numbers (median 6.45%, growth-period 15.38%, max 40%) and the 18-day embayment clearance estimate.

title: Feeding reduction, reproductive failure, and mortality in Mytilus edulis during the 1985 'brown tide' in Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island
result: Clearance normal below 2.5×10⁵ bloom particles/mL and reduced above 5×10⁵.
env_effects: 30-100% mussel mortality along the bay, with complete reproductive failure.

title: Uptake kinetics of paralytic shellfish toxins from the dinoflagellate Alexandrium fundyense in the mussel Mytilus edulis
organism: mussel → Alexandrium fundyense vs Thalassiosira weissflogii
result: Clearance on Alexandrium ~48% lower than on the diatom; toxin passed the 80 µg STXeq/100 g limit in <1 h; 79% of ingested toxin kept.
env_effects: No mussel mortality over 17 d; animals became toxic.

title: Influence of dinoflagellate cell toxicity on uptake and loss of paralytic shellfish toxins in the northern quahog Mercenaria mercenaria
organism: hard clam → two Alexandrium isolates (+ T. weissflogii)
result: Clams ate the high-toxicity strain only with diatom added; tissues exceeded the closure level 'by several orders of magnitude'.
env_effects: Toxin depurated over 3-6 weeks.

title: Experimental and Histological Studies of Four Life-History Stages of the Eastern Oyster, Crassostrea virginica, Exposed to a Cultured Strain of the Dinoflagellate Prorocentrum minimum
result: Juvenile oysters filtered P. minimum but rejected most as pseudofeces for ~2 weeks before digesting it.
env_effects: Larvae grew poorly on P. minimum.

title: Hepatotoxic shellfish poisoning: Accumulation of microcystins in Eastern oysters (Crassostrea virginica) and Asian clams (Corbicula fluminea) exposed to wild and cultured populations of the harmful cyanobacteria, Microcystis
scale: lab 1 L beakers: cultured Microcystis LE-3 (10^6 cells/mL) for 3 d and Lake Agawam NY bloom water (cyanobacteria 118 and 71 ug Chl-a/L; microcystin 38 and 29 ug/L) for 4 d
dose: 10^6 cells/mL cultured Microcystis (single and double cells) vs colonial bloom water
result: On cultured Microcystis, clam tissue microcystin fell from 3668 ng/g at 24 h to 719 ng/g at 72 h as clearance dropped, while oyster tissue rose to 4905 ng/g at 72 h with steady clearance; on colonial bloom water accumulation was only up to 2 ng/g.
env_effects: Both bivalves exceeded the California guidance value (10 ng/g) by orders of magnitude on cultured cells; oysters did not depurate over 3-4 days and are the likelier vector of hepatotoxic shellfish poisoning.
key_details: Lab clearance, particle-selection and toxin-accumulation experiments with Asian clams (Corbicula fluminea) and eastern oysters using toxic Microcystis culture (Lake Erie LE-3) and bloom water from Lake Agawam, NY. Clams cleared Microcystis faster than a green alga in culture, but in bloom water both bivalves cleared more slowly and clams selected green algae over cyanobacteria. Clams accumulated microcystin rapidly (3668 ng/g at 24 h) and then depurated to 719 ng/g by 72 h while clearance fell; oysters kept a steady ~0.11 L/h clearance and rose to 4905 ng/g by 72 h. On colonial bloom water accumulation stayed at or below 2 ng/g. The focus is shellfish safety, not bloom control.

title: Seston Removal by Natural and Constructed Intertidal Eastern Oyster (Crassostrea virginica) Reefs: A Comparison with Previous Laboratory Studies, and the Value of in situ Methods
organism: intertidal oyster reefs (Crassostrea virginica dominant; hard clams on one reef; few ribbed mussels) -> chl a
scale: 8 intertidal reefs (5 constructed, 3 natural), coastal South Carolina; flow lengths 5-18 m
duration: 0.3-1.3 h measurement runs, May 2005 and June 2006
result: In situ fluorometry showed chl a removal from -9.8% to 27.9% (lab pumped samples -9.3% to 40.7%) across reefs; overall means 12.9% (in situ) and 13.6% (lab).
env_effects: One natural reef showed higher chl a downstream from wind-driven sediment resuspension. Bare planted shell with no live oysters removed no chl a.
key_details: Upstream-downstream in situ fluorometry plus pumped water samples over 8 intertidal South Carolina reefs in shallow water (26-42 cm depth, flow 2.2-13.5 cm/s), bivalve densities 217-2831 per m2. Removal averaged ~13% across reefs; two older reefs removed 15.1% and 23.0%, one young reef 21.8%, and two reefs <5%. A bare-shell control showed no physical removal. Predicted removal matched measured (11.7% vs 12.9%) only when Powell et al. 'low gear' individual feeding rates were used; lab-derived rates overpredict. Each run was a single short time series per reef (no replicate reefs per treatment).
fulltext_discrepancy: Record gave only the range; the overall mean removal (12.9% in situ, 13.6% lab) and the finding that lab-derived clearance rates overpredict field removal were missing.

title: Can oyster restoration reverse cultural eutrophication in Chesapeake Bay?
result: Summer surface chl fell only about 1 mg/m³.
env_effects: Deep DO +0.25 g/m³; SAV +20%; oysters a supplement to, not a substitute for, nutrient cuts.

title: Denitrification and nutrient assimilation on a restored oyster reef
result: NH4⁺, SRP and O2 fluxes ≥10× the control in every season; denitrification 0.3-1.6 mmol N m⁻² h⁻¹.
env_effects: Ammonium and phosphate release ≥10× control.

title: Role of Shellfish Aquaculture in the Reduction of Eutrophication in an Urban Estuary
result: System-scale model: oyster aquaculture removes 1.31% (current) and 2.68% (expanded, 1,340 t N/yr) of annual N inputs to Long Island Sound; modelled Chl reduction by filtration averaged 1.3% (current) and 2.1% (expanded), max 5.3% in one box; farm-scale model showed 0.3% Chl drop.
env_effects: N-removal valued at $8.5M (current) to $470M (max expanded) per year in avoided costs. Optimistic all-lease estimate incl. denitrification: 10-30% of N inputs.
key_details: Modelling study (EcoWin/EWN system model, FARM local model, ASSETS eutrophication index) for Connecticut oyster leases in Long Island Sound, plus avoided-cost valuation. No field manipulation. Oysters cleared 0.95x (current) to 2.08x (expanded) the cultivated-box volume per year. Model overestimates Chl because it lacks zooplankton grazers. Clams, NY leases and denitrification excluded from the base numbers.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record lacked the chlorophyll outcome: filtration lowered modelled Chl only 1.3-2.1% on average, the relevant bloom-control number.

title: Benthic Filter Feeding: A Natural Eutrophication Control
result: Control works when the benthic water-recycling time ≈ the phytoplankton growth time constant; favoured by shallow water and dense small animals.
env_effects: Not reported.

title: Assessment of filtration capacity of different bivalve species suitable for integrated multi-trophic aquaculture (IMTA) systems vis-à-vis waste valorization for sustainable environment
organism: blood clam Tegillarca granosa, oyster Crassostrea madrasensis, green mussel Perna viridis feeding on Thalassiosira sp. (microcosm) and shrimp-farm wastewater (mesocosm)
scale: 9 x 5 L microcosms (1 bivalve per 2 L) and 9 x 300 L tanks with 50 L shrimp wastewater (2 bivalves per 50 L)
result: Plankton removal 94% (clam) / 87.1% (oyster) / 77.0% (mussel); species not significantly different.
env_effects: Mesocosm: similar clearance of ammonia, nitrite, phosphate, BOD, TDS across species; oysters removed more COD and TSS; total bacteria lowest with green mussels.
key_details: Lab study from Kakinada, India, 5 days, each species in triplicate (3 species x 3 = 9 units in each setting). Plankton counted daily (Sedgewick-Rafter) and Chl-a measured; filtration and clearance rates calculated. Plankton filtration efficiency 94% (clam), 87.1% (oyster), 77.0% (mussel), not significantly different. There is no bivalve-free control, so settling or die-off of Thalassiosira is not separated from filtration.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record correct on numbers; key caveat missing: no no-bivalve control, so the 77-94% removals are not controlled.

title: Effect of yellow loess on clearance rate in seven species of benthic, filter-feeding invertebrates
result: Oyster clearance unaffected until 1.0 g/L loess; mussels affected at 1-10 g/L; scallop clearance down at 0.01 g/L.
env_effects: Not reported.
